options: Subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin) or fondaparinux
Thrombolysis with alteplase
IV nicardipine
Immediate angiography with stenting within 2 hours
Discharge with an outpatient exercise test

set.explanation: A 30-year smoker with cough, chest pain, rapid weight loss, finger clubbing and a peripheral mass with an effusion has lung cancer, and clubbing (with or without hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy) is characteristic of non-small cell types – squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma – but uncommon in small cell carcinoma, which is typically central with early metastases and endocrine syndromes. Mesothelioma is usually linked to asbestos exposure and causes diffuse or nodular pleural thickening with effusion rather than a discrete peripheral lung mass, while asbestosis and coal worker's pneumoconiosis are fibrotic or nodular diseases without a mass or rapid weight loss. CT staging, tissue diagnosis and molecular testing come next.

options: Increased FEV1/FVC ratio, decreased TLC, decreased DLCO
Decreased FEV1/FVC ratio, increased TLC, increased RV, decreased DLCO
Normal FEV1/FVC ratio, decreased TLC, normal DLCO
Normal lung volumes, normal DLCO, normal FEV1/FVC ratio
Decreased FEV1/FVC ratio, normal TLC, increased DLCO
set.explanation: COPD is obstructive: FEV1 falls more than FVC, so the FEV1/FVC ratio is below 0.70. Loss of elastic recoil and airway collapse cause gas trapping (raised RV) and hyperinflation (raised TLC), and emphysematous alveolar destruction lowers DLCO. A reduced TLC with a normal or high ratio indicates restriction, a raised DLCO suggests alveolar haemorrhage, polycythaemia or asthma, and normal results would not fit symptomatic COPD. A low ratio with a normal or raised DLCO suggests asthma.

PEF 33–50%, RR ≥25/min and HR ≥110/min define acute severe asthma; with SpO2 still ≥92% and no exhaustion or silent chest there is no life-threatening feature. First-line treatment is repeated high-dose nebulised (or spacer) salbutamol, with ipratropium if the response is poor, controlled oxygen now to keep SpO2 94–98% (his is 93% on air), and an early systemic corticosteroid (prednisolone 40–50 mg daily for at least 5 days). IV magnesium is reserved for a poor response to initial bronchodilators or life-threatening features, and maintenance changes (ICS–formoterol, LAMA, montelukast) are made once the attack is controlled, before discharge.

A rising high-sensitivity troponin with dynamic ST depression is an NSTEMI, which is a high-risk feature; if the patient is stable and pain-free, early coronary angiography within 24 hours is recommended (ESC 2023). Immediate angiography within 2 hours is for very high-risk features: refractory pain, haemodynamic instability, arrhythmia or acute heart failure. Fibrinolysis is not used without ST elevation, and moderate CKD (eGFR 32, stage G3b) calls for isotonic hydration and a minimal contrast volume, not a delay.

set.stem: A 73-year-old woman has chest discomfort and a slow pulse of 53/min with occasional pauses. Her ECG shows sinus bradycardia with intermittent pauses of 3 seconds in which no P wave appears. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Echocardiography and an ECG (voltage criteria, strain pattern) confirm LVH.

options: Negative stress test; inappropriate hypertensive response to exercise
Negative stress test; nonspecific ST changes
Nondiagnostic stress test; normal blood pressure response
Positive stress test; inappropriate hypertensive response to exercise
Positive stress test; normal blood pressure response

In a patient with STEMI presenting to a centre without percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) capability, what is the preferred reperfusion strategy?

P waves

set.stem: Ms. Wilson is a 66-year-old postmenopausal U.S. postal employee. While walking her mail route over the past 9 months, she has routinely experienced chest pressure and dyspnoea while climbing a certain steep hill. The pressure resolves when she rests for about 3 minutes. She has not missed any work due to these symptoms. You suspect she is experiencing angina. What term and Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) Functional Class of angina is appropriate to describe her symptoms?

A 67-year-old fry chef at the local waffle house presents to the emergency department with the sudden onset of crushing substernal chest pain. He has a history of hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and erectile dysfunction for which he takes daily amlodipine, simvastatin, and tadalafil. On your evaluation, his blood pressure is 145/85 mmHg, and heart rate is 90 bpm. His lungs are clear, and jugular venous pulse is not elevated. There are no murmurs or gallops on cardiac auscultation. He continues to complain of chest discomfort, rating it an 8/10. Initial troponin I result is elevated at 0.52 ng/dL (normal <0.06 ng/dL), and ECG reveals 1-mm ST depression in leads II, III, aVF, V5, and V6. All of the following pharmacologic therapies are reasonable to administer EXCEPT:

options: Anticoagulation with warfarin is superior to antiplatelet agents in preventing adverse cardiovascular events in patients with PAD
B-Adrenergic blockers have been shown to worsen limb ischaemia and should not be used in PAD
He should exercise daily, walking to the point of maximal claudication before stopping to rest and allowing his symptoms to resolve
His greatest risk of morbidity and mortality over the ensuing 5 years is progression to critical limb ischaemia
Vasodilators are first-line therapy for symptomatic PAD
More men than women suffer from varicose veins
More men than women suffer from chronic venous insufficiency with oedema
More than 50% of patients over 70 years old have chronic venous insufficiency
Most patients with chronic venous insufficiency will develop venous ulcers
All of the above are true

set.stem: You are evaluating a 77-year-old woman from Ohio with a history of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, diabetes mellitus, and a prior left lower extremity deep venous thrombosis treated with anticoagulation. For the past several months, she has complained of a cramping, burning sensation in her legs. Today she presents for evaluation of a skin ulcer, as shown. On examination, there is ulceration over the medial malleolus with nonpitting woody oedema and skin hyperpigmentation. This ulcer is most likely due to which of the following?

A 64-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the sudden onset of substernal chest pain and nausea while playing tennis. He has hypertension and hyperlipidaemia. Current medications include hydrochlorothiazide and atorvastatin. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. He is diaphoretic and distressed. Pulse is 110/min, respirations are 31/min, and blood pressure is 85/55 mm Hg. Examination shows jugular venous distention. Crackles are heard over the lower lung fields bilaterally. Capillary refill time is delayed; the extremities are cool to touch. A 12-lead ECG shows ST elevations in leads II, III, and aVF. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

A 30-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of progressive effort intolerance and an episode of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea three weeks ago. Her past medical history is negative for hypertension or diabetes. On examination, her jugular venous pressure is elevated up to her earlobes, she has a soft, tender hepatomegaly, bilateral pitting oedema up to the knees, bibasal crepitations, and an audible S3 on cardiac auscultation. A chest X-ray reveals cardiomegaly with interstitial infiltrates, and echocardiography shows global left ventricular hypokinesia with an ejection fraction of 25–30%. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options: Thromboembolism
Oesophageal varices
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Myocardial infarction
Liver cirrhosis

set.stem: A 67-year-old man with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and ischaemic heart disease is taken to the Emergency Department with dyspnoea. On examination his respiratory rate is 24/min JVP is not elevated and crackles are heard in both lung bases. Which other finding would most strongly indicate that his dyspnoea is secondary to isolated left ventricular failure?

A 75-year-old man presents to your emergency department appearing quite ill. His family says he has not had his normal energy for the last 6 months, and they noted he was confused and lethargic for the last day or two. As you take a history from the family, you palpate the patient’s radial pulse and notice a regular beat-to-beat variability of pulse amplitude, although his rhythm is regular. Indeed, as you later take his blood pressure, you note that only every other phase I (systolic) Korotkoff sound is audible as the cuff pressure is slowly lowered and that this is independent of the respiratory cycle. Based on this, you suspect this patient has which of the following?

A 78-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit with decompensated heart failure. He has longstanding ischaemic cardiomyopathy. ECG shows atrial fibrillation and left bundle branch block. Chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly and bilateral alveolar infiltrates with Kerley B lines. Which of the following is least likely to be present on physical examination?

A 71-year-old woman with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 38% has been hospitalized for the past week with acute decompensated heart failure. After diuresis and medication optimization, she is feeling immensely better. She is on the maximally tolerated doses of an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, B-blocker, and appropriate diuretic dose. You are planning for discharge today. On rounds, the nurse notes that the patient had several short (5-10 beats) runs of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT) and multiple premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) overnight, although she remained asymptomatic. A medical student on the team asks if the NSVT carries any prognostic significance and if any intervention is needed. What is the most appropriate response?

A 68-year-old man with a history of myocardial infarction and congestive heart failure is comfortable at rest. However, when walking to his car, he develops dyspnoea, fatigue, and sometimes palpitations. He must rest for several minutes before these symptoms resolve. Which of the following is his New York Heart Association classification?

A 47-year-old postmenopausal woman is seen for onset of severe dyspnoea over the last few weeks. She reports no preceding chest pain, cough, sputum, or fever, although she does report leg swelling. Physical examination is notable for a blood pressure of 145/78 mmHg and heart rate of 123 bpm. Exophthalmos is present, as well as bilateral inspiratory crackles occupying approximately one-third of the lower chest with neck vein distention. She has a third heart sound with no murmur. Bilateral lower extremity oedema is also present, with warm extremities and a fine hand tremor. Which of the following is the most likely pathophysiologic explanation for her heart failure?
options: Anaemia with high-output state
Chronic systemic hypertension with resultant left ventricular hypertrophy and nonsystolic heart failure
Hemochromatosis with subsequent restrictive cardiomyopathy
Myocardial infarction with depressed left ventricular systolic function
Thyrotoxicosis with high-output state
Angiotensin II
B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP)
Calcium uptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Norepinephrine
Tumour necrosis factor

set.stem: Mr. George is a 52-year-old man with long standing hypertension and poorly controlled diabetes. He presents complaining of several months of breathlessness with exertion, acute episodes of shortness of breath when recumbent, and lower extremity oedema. On examination, he has an elevated jugular venous pulse and an S4 on auscultation. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55% with a large left atrium. You suspect this patient has the syndrome of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Drugs targeting which of the following have convincingly demonstrated mortality reduction for patients with HFpEF?

You are evaluating a 64-year-old woman with a history of nonischaemic cardiomyopathy. She presents to the emergency department for shortness of breath. You note that she has gained 11 kg since her last cardiology appointment 2 months ago. Physical examination confirms findings associated with acute decompensated heart failure, including pulmonary rales, elevated jugular venous pulse, abdominal ascites, lower extremity oedema, and a square wave blood pressure Valsalva response. Her extremities are warm, and blood pressure is 110/78 mmHg with a heart rate of 75 bpm. Her laboratory studies return with a sodium of 128 mEq/L and creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL (which is increased from her prior level of 1.2 mg/dL). Chest x-ray shows a diffuse alveolar filling pattern consistent with pulmonary oedema. What is the next most appropriate step?
Which of the following statements regarding nesiritide is true in patients with acute decompensated heart failure requiring invasive haemodynamic monitoring?

options: Decreased transpulmonary pressure
Decreased minute ventilation
Increase pulmonary capillary pressure
Increased pulmonary capillary permeability
Decreased total body haemoglobin

set.stem: A 66-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and diabetes presents with a 3-week history of exertional dyspnoea. Cardiac exam reveals an S3 gallop. What further evaluation is most likely to show?

A 34-year-old woman is referred by an OB- GYN colleague for the onset of fatigue and dyspnoea on exertion 1 month after her second vaginal delivery. Physical examination reveals a laterally displaced PMI, elevated jugular venous pressure and 2+ pitting lower extremity oedema. Echocardiogram shows systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 30%. Which statement most accurately describes her condition?

Chest x-ray shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields. Which of the following would be the best initial diagnostic approach?

Rib notching
Pulmonary oedema
Hyperlucent lung fields

set.stem: Two weeks after hospital discharge for documented myocardial infarction, a 65-year-old returns to your office concerned about low-grade fever and pleuritic chest pain. There is no associated shortness of breath. Lungs are clear to auscultation and the heart is free of murmur, gallop, or rub. ECG is unchanged from the last one in the hospital. Which therapy is most likely to be effective?

options: Myocardial infarction
Aortic dissection
Pulmonary embolism
Pericarditis

set.stem: A 67-year-old male presents to your office after community ultrasound screening revealed an aortic aneurysm measuring 3.0 × 3.5 cm. Physical examination confirms a palpable, pulsatile, nontender abdominal mass just above the umbilicus. The patient’s medical conditions include hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and tobacco use. What is the best recommendation for the patient to consider?

set.stem: A 66-year-old heavy smoker presents with chronic productive cough, progressive dyspnoea, pursed-lip breathing, and a barrel chest. What is the most likely diagnosis?
